https://www.dw.com/en/zambia-suspends-vo.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5IpFh The commission said there had been instances where ​marked ballot papers in ballot boxes ⁠had ​been ​stolen Image: Moses Mwape/REUTERS Advertisement Zambia 's electoral commission has suspended the counting and announcement of election results nationwide with immediate effect, citing violence directed at election officials. The commission said ballot papers had also been stolen in some cases and that it would review the suspension within 24 hours. Why has Zambia suspended vote counting? The Electoral Commission of Zambia said the decision followed incidents of violence targeting polling staff. It added that ballot papers had been stolen in some locations, though it did not immediately give details on where the incidents occurred or how widespread they were. The general election is a major test for President Hakainde Hichilema, whose economic reform program has been weighed against widespread frustration over the cost of living. Around 8 million people were registered to vote in the southern African country of about 22 million people. Can Zambia trust election referee? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Voters were also choosing members of parliament and local councillors at more than 13,500 polling stations. Were there problems during voting? Long queues formed before dawn at polling stations in Lusaka, with some voters gathering around makeshift fires as they waited. Local observers reported delays and frustration at some polling stations because of poor voter guidance, confusion over voter rolls and crowd-management problems. European Union observers were monitoring the election. Hichilema came to power in 2021 after defeating longtime rival Edgar Lungu , who served as president from 2015 to 2021 and died in 2025. Lungu's political legacy still looms over the election, with Hichilema's main challenger Brian Mundubile leading an opposition alliance backed by many of the former president's supporters. Photograph: Social media/Reuters Saudi Arabia Riyadh airport hit again after deadly Houthi missile attack, Saudi authorities say Unidentified projectile strikes King Khalid airport as escalating attacks threaten to draw more countries into Yemen conflict Middle East crisis live – latest updates Analysis: attack will force rethink of Trump strategy William Christou in Jerusalem Sun 11 Oct 2026 12.49 EDT First published on Sun 11 Oct 2026 10.23 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A projectile hit a passenger terminal at the airport in Riyadh on Sunday, the day after a deadly missile attack on the facility carried out by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebel group killed 13 people. An unidentified projectile hit terminal 4 at King Khalid international airport, starting a fire and causing injuries, according to Saudi authorities. Air defences also intercepted a cruise missile in the vicinity of the airport. It was the latest of several attacks on the airport in the past week. The escalating attacks threatened to draw more countries into the Yemen conflict and further widen the regional fallout of the US-Iran war, which has already spread to Lebanon and Iraq. After Saturday’s strike on Riyadh airport, the US president, Donald Trump, said he was weighing whether to join the Saudi military campaign in Yemen, telling reporters: “We’re going to look into it.” The Iran-allied Houthis claimed to have launched several attacks on the airport, including the attack on Saturday, which killed 13 people and injured more than 300 – the deadliest attack on a Gulf country since the war with Iran started in March and an apparent escalation in the Houthis’ war with Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government that Riyadh sponsors. Regional map In response to the attack, Saudi authorities extended the closure of the airport and said schools would be moved online until Thursday. The Houthis claimed that Saudi Arabia struck the airport in Yemen’s rebel-held capital, Sana’a, on Sunday, without providing more information on damage or casualties. Videos circulated on social media showing travellers walking through debris-strewn ground in the Riyadh airport as sirens blared. Four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshi nationals, a Palestinian, a US citizen, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Syrian and a Sudanese were killed in the missile strike. On Saturday night, the spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen, Maj Gen Turki al-Maliki, said the coalition would “respond firmly” to the attack, offering few other details. Aftermath of strike on Riyadh’s international airport The Houthis said a Saudi airstrike on Sana’a on Sunday hit a home and killed a child, as well as injuring six others. The Houthis doubled down on their threats on Sunday, warning airlines, passengers and staff to stay away from Saudi airports. The group said “the worst is yet to come” if Saudi military action in Yemen continued. “We renew our warning to all airlines, experts, employees, workers and travellers against using Saudi airports and airspace, as they are vulnerable to attack and have become a theatre of operations for our forces,” the Houthis said in a statement on X. Trump said he would speak to the Saudi crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman, on Saturday night, after the previous attack on the airport. The US has already been assisting with intelligence cooperation and targeting, with about 200 US military advisers stationed in Saudi Arabia to help with the campaign. Until now, the US has not directly taken part in fighting against the Houthis. Direct US involvement could lead the group to resume its targeting of ships passing through the Bab al-Mandab strait, through which about 10% of global maritime goods transit. View image in fullscreen People outside a metro station on the road to King Khalid international airport in Riyadh on Saturday. Photograph: AP It would also further entangle the US in Middle East wars as the American public grows increasingly frustrated with the continuing Iran conflict. Trump faces the prospect of midterm elections in November with an unpopular war and soaring prices at home, threatening his party’s performance at the polls. Saudi Arabia is already carrying out airstrikes against the Houthis in Yemen. The Houthi government’s health ministry said coalition airstrikes over the last six weeks had killed 91 Yemenis and wounded 168, 60% of whom it said were women and children. Saudi-backed government forces in Yemen launched a campaign to push the Houthis back from the areas the group conquered over the last month. Despite claiming initial successes, the government forces have not been able to loosen the Houthis’ grip over areas closest to the Bab al-Mandab strait such as Perim Island. The Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia said one of its citizens died on Sunday after being wounded in the Riyadh airport attack a day earlier. The Egyptian woman killed in the attack on the airport was a flight attendant identified as Azza Ramzy, 28, who worked for the Saudi airline Flynas, according to Egyptian state-run TV. The Syrian woman was a widowed mother of four who had been living in Saudi Arabia for five years, a relative told the Associated Press. The Syrian embassy in Riyadh identified her as Buthaina Ahmad Oweida. Her niece, Nisreen Oweida, said her aunt was 56, from Syria’s northern Idlib province, and had left during the country’s civil war. She was living in Mecca and had been returning from a visit to her sister in Riyadh when she was killed, the niece said. The airport attack was met with a wave of international condemnation, including from the UN secretary general, António Guterres, and the president of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen. “Attacks by Iran’s proxies are pushing the region into a spiral of violence,” von der Leyen wrote on X. “They are destabilising crucial global transport and energy nodes.” The increasing intensity of Houthi attacks against Riyadh and its energy infrastructure has brought more foreign involvement in the Yemen war. Governments are facing pressure over oil prices, already high from the US-Iran war since March. On Monday, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey issued a joint statement saying they would move quickly to implement their mutual defence pact, including by speeding up the deployment of military forces in the kingdom. The UK said it would assist with defensive military support of Riyadh, providing refuelling for aircraft working to intercept Houthi missiles into Riyadh. Saudi Arabia has asked for further assistance from France, Egypt, the UK and Pakistan as its stock of interceptor missiles are running low. View image in fullscreen Houthi supporters rally in Sana’a on Friday. Photograph: Yahya Arhab/EPA The Houthis launched a military campaign to take Yemen’s Red Sea coast in early September after months of escalating tensions with the Yemeni government and its Saudi patron. The campaign interrupted years of relative calm in the country after a 2022 UN-brokered ceasefire froze frontlines between the Houthis and the government. Despite the Saudi-supported counteroffensive, the group seems to have held on to its recent gains. It is unclear what further Saudi military action would look like against the Houthis, who resisted years of strikes by an international coalition, as well as by the US. Saudi Arabia led an international coalition that intervened against the Houthis in Yemen in 2015 after the group took over Sana’a and toppled the Yemeni government. Recent Houthi attacks against Saudi energy infrastructure, as well as Houthi military advances, have pulled Saudi Arabia back into the Yemen war. https://www.politico.eu/article/islam-sh.text: BERLIN — Alice Weidel sees her far-right Alternative for Germany as the country’s new mainstream party. That doesn’t mean she’s moderating her message. In a wide-ranging interview, the co-leader of the AfD — Germany’s most popular party — called for the departure of millions of migrants and accused Germany’s Central Council of Jews of taking its marching orders from Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s Christian Democrats. She also took aim at Marine Le Pen, accusing the far-right French presidential candidate of isolating her own party on the European right by bashing Germany. Advertisement Advertisement “Yes, I’m keeping my fingers crossed for Ms. Le Pen,” Weidel said during an interview with a new weekly video podcast from WELT published Friday. WELT, like POLITICO, is part of the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network. But Weidel bristled at Le Pen’s call this week for a “Europe of nations” to replace a “German Europe.” The leader of France’s far-right National Rally party had “perhaps misunderstood something, or doesn’t see how the money flows,” Weidel said, referring to Germany paying the largest portion of the EU budget. The relationship between the two parties has been cold since Le Pen cut ties with the AfD in 2024, after one of the AfD’s leading politicians told an Italian newspaper that not every SS member was automatically a criminal. Among Europe’s “patriotic” parties, “it is not the AfD that is isolated, but increasingly the National Rally, if it carries on like this,” she added. Weidel also rejected Le Pen’s contention in a television appearance in October that Islam, unlike Sharia, is compatible with the French Republic: “Islam is Sharia and Sharia is Islam.” Le Pen has worked to rid the party of the racist and antisemitic reputation it developed under her father, Jean-Marie, who was convicted multiple times for racist comments and downplaying the Holocaust. On the subject of expelling migrants from Germany, Weidel outbid her AfD co-leader Tino Chrupalla, who recently put the number of people who should leave Germany at 2.6 million. Advertisement Advertisement “Frankly, the number is much larger,” she said, and listed whom she meant: the roughly 250,000 people already obliged to leave the country as well as violent offenders, Islamists and others who “hang around in our social hammock, live an easy life here and don’t integrate.” She added those whose protection she would revoke once the reason for fleeing no longer applies — “completely, entirely, all” 900,000 Syrians, all Afghans and, after a peace deal, 1.1 million Ukrainians. On Ukraine, Weidel doubled down on her claim that Kyiv had already lost the war. If she were in Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s shoes, she would recommend “immediately flying to Russia and sitting down at the table with Putin.” She added: “I would do it.” Weidel dismissed the suggestion that a Russian victory would trigger another wave of refugees heading west. “There will be no refugee movement. Quite the opposite,” she said, arguing that Ukrainians in Germany would return home once peace was established “because they are needed there.” Weidel was more evasive on the subject of Israel. Asked about a now-deleted post by AfD lawmaker Kay Gottschalk stating there is no “right to exist” for any nation, Weidel called it “botched.” Advertisement Advertisement Asked directly whether Israel has a right to exist, she said, “As a German party, what befits us first and foremost is defending Germany’s sovereignty. That is in our national interest.” Then, “to answer your question directly”: anyone who looks at the AfD’s motions in the Bundestag over the past ten years “will see who stands at Israel’s side.” The AfD, she added, is “the only and last protective power of Jewish life in Germany.” Asked why, then, the Central Council of Jews in Germany warns against her party, Weidel claimed the organization had been politicized by the CDU. “It is permanently being used as a weapon against the AfD,” she said, offering no evidence. Council President Josef Schuster has repeatedly warned that an AfD government would endanger Jewish life in Germany, citing the party’s positions on religious practices and its politicians’ remarks about the Nazi era. The Council did not immediately respond to a request for comment. In a statement provided to POLITICO after publication, Schuster described Weidel’s allegation as “absurd.” “For years, the AfD has been searching for a fig leaf for its resentment-laden politics, while at the same time seeking to restrict freedom of religion and to destroy the consensus on the politics of remembrance,” he said. “The Jewish community in Germany will not provide it with that fig leaf.” In September, Weidel declared that the AfD had supplanted the Christian Democrats as Germany’s traditional people’s party — meaning a party with broad appeal across society . Advertisement Advertisement For all her attacks on the Christian Democrats, Weidel made clear she was still open to working with them. The CDU, which she no longer considers a center-right party, was “destroying itself behind the firewall,” she said, referring to the longstanding agreement by Germany’s establishment parties not to work with the far right. Her hand, she said, remains “outstretched.” UPDATED: This article was update on Nov. 11 with a comment from Schuster. Marc Felix Serra o is a Global Reporter with The Axel Springer Global Reporters Network and co-host of “Zur Wahrheit gehört” (“Part of the Truth”), a new weekly video podcast from WELT. The Axel Springer Global Reporters Network harnesses the resources of the company’s newsrooms to publish ambitious scoops, investigations, interviews, opinion pieces and analysis.
